sections.title: I. Investment Company Act of 1940 — Classification & Framework
sections.overview: The Investment Company Act of 1940 defines and regulates entities engaged primarily in investing, reinvesting, or trading in securities. It divides investment companies into three statutory classes and further subclassifies management companies by capital structure (open vs. closed-end) and portfolio composition (diversified vs. non-diversified).
key_concepts: Investment company definition: issuer engaged primarily in investing/reinvesting/trading in securities, OR issues face-amount certificates, OR holds investment securities >40% of total assets (excl. Government securities and cash).
Three statutory classes under §4: (1) Face-Amount Certificate Company, (2) Unit Investment Trust (UIT), (3) Management Company.
UIT characteristics: organized under trust indenture, NO board of directors, issues only redeemable securities representing an undivided interest in a fixed (unmanaged) portfolio; not a voting trust.

Management companies subdivided under §5(a) into Open-End (issues redeemable securities — mutual funds) and Closed-End (any management company that is not open-end; issues fixed share count, trades in secondary market).
Diversified vs. Non-diversified under §5(b): the 75-5-10 test — at least 75% of assets meeting limits of no more than 5% in any one issuer and no more than 10% of voting securities of any one issuer.
Excluded from 'investment securities': Government securities, employees' securities companies, and majority-owned non-investment-company subsidiaries.
Private fund safe-harbor signal under §3(c)(1): securities beneficially owned by ≤100 persons and no public offering.
rules: Investment Company Act of 1940 §3(a) — definition; 40% asset test.
Investment Company Act of 1940 §4 — three classes: FAC, UIT, management company.
Investment Company Act of 1940 §5(a) — open-end vs. closed-end.
Investment Company Act of 1940 §5(b) — diversified vs. non-diversified (75-5-10).
formulas: 40% Test = (Investment securities) / (Total assets − Government securities − cash items) > 40% → investment company.
Diversification Test (75-5-10): ≥75% of assets meeting (≤5% in any one issuer) AND (≤10% of voting securities of any one issuer).
mnemonics: FUM = Face-amount, UIT, Management (the three §4 classes).
75-5-10 = '75 cents of every dollar diversified, 5% per issuer max, 10% of voting max.'
Open-end = Ongoing redemption; Closed-end = Capped shares.

sections.title: II. Open-End Funds (Mutual Funds)
sections.overview: Open-end funds (mutual funds) continuously issue and redeem shares at the next computed net asset value (forward pricing). Shares are not traded on exchanges; investors buy from and redeem with the fund. Pricing, sales loads, share classes, and distribution fees are tightly regulated under the '40 Act.
key_concepts: Continuous primary offering; shares are redeemable securities issued by the fund.
Forward pricing: orders execute at the NEXT calculated NAV (typically end of business day, 4:00 p.m. ET).
POP (Public Offering Price) = NAV + sales charge (for funds with front-end loads).
Share classes: Class A (front-end load, lower 12b-1), Class B (back-end CDSC, declining; convert to A) — now largely phased out, Class C (level load, higher ongoing 12b-1, typically no/short CDSC).
12b-1 fees: ongoing asset-based distribution/marketing fees deducted from fund assets pursuant to a written 12b-1 plan; reduce return.
Breakpoints: discounted sales charges at specified investment thresholds; FINRA prohibits 'breakpoint sales' just below thresholds.
Letter of Intent (LOI): written commitment to invest enough within 13 months to qualify for a breakpoint; may be backdated up to 90 days.
Right of Accumulation (ROA): existing holdings count toward new breakpoint qualification; no time limit.
FINRA caps maximum aggregate sales charges on open-end fund shares at 8.5% (with conditions including breakpoints, ROA, and reinvested dividends at NAV).
Tailored Shareholder Reports (TSRs): open-end funds must deliver concise TSRs to retail shareholders (Rule 30e-3 rescinded for open-end funds; compliance 7/24/2024).
Prospectus delivery required at or before sale; summary prospectus permitted.
rules: 17 CFR 270.12b-1 — distribution fees by open-end management investment companies.
FINRA Rule 2342 — prohibition of breakpoint sales just below the breakpoint.
Investment Company Act of 1940 §5(a)(1) — open-end definition.
formulas: NAV per share = (Total Fund Assets − Total Fund Liabilities) / Shares Outstanding.
Public Offering Price (POP) = NAV / (1 − Sales Charge %).
Sales Charge % = (POP − NAV) / POP.
Redemption Price (no CDSC) = NAV at next computed price.
mnemonics: ABC shares: A = Anterior load (front), B = Back-end CDSC, C = Constant level load.
LOI = 'Locked-In 13 months, 90-day backdate.'
Forward Pricing = 'Order first, Price second.'

sections.title: III. Closed-End Funds & UITs
sections.overview: Closed-end funds (CEFs) issue a fixed number of shares in an IPO and trade on exchanges at market prices that can diverge from NAV (premium or discount). Unit Investment Trusts (UITs) hold a fixed, unmanaged portfolio and issue redeemable units representing undivided interests.
key_concepts: Closed-end: fixed capitalization after IPO; shares trade intraday on an exchange at supply/demand-driven market price.
CEF market price may trade at a premium or discount to NAV; no continuous redemption.
CEFs may use leverage and may issue debt or preferred stock (open-end funds may not issue senior securities other than narrowly permitted bank borrowings).
UITs: no board of directors, no investment adviser actively managing the portfolio; trust terminates on a stated date.
UIT units are redeemable; sponsor typically maintains a secondary market.
UITs often used as packaged fixed-portfolio vehicles (e.g., fixed-income or equity unit trusts).
rules: Investment Company Act of 1940 §4(2) — UIT definition (trust indenture, no board, redeemable undivided interests).
Investment Company Act of 1940 §5(a)(2) — closed-end definition.
formulas: Premium/Discount % = (Market Price − NAV) / NAV × 100.
mnemonics: CEF = 'Capped, Exchange-listed, Fluctuating premium/discount.'
UIT = 'Unmanaged, Indenture, Terminates.'

sections.title: IV. Money Market Mutual Funds (Rule 2a-7)
sections.overview: Money market funds are open-end funds investing in short-term, high-quality instruments and are regulated under Rule 2a-7. The 2023 SEC reforms restructured liquidity safeguards: gates were eliminated and a mandatory liquidity fee was introduced for institutional prime/tax-exempt funds.
key_concepts: Fund types: Government MMFs and Retail MMFs (stable $1.00 NAV via amortized cost/penny-rounding); Institutional Prime and Institutional Tax-Exempt MMFs (floating NAV).
Minimum Daily Liquid Assets: 25%.
Minimum Weekly Liquid Assets: 50%.
Mandatory liquidity fee: institutional prime and institutional tax-exempt MMFs must impose a fee when daily net redemptions exceed 5% of NAV (compliance 10/2/2024).
Discretionary liquidity fee: up to 2% for non-government MMFs at board discretion.
Redemption gates were eliminated by the 2023 reforms (SEC Rel. IC-34959).
Portfolio constraints: short weighted average maturity, high credit quality, diversification.
rules: SEC Rel. IC-34959 (2023 MMF reforms) — mandatory fee, 25%/50% liquidity thresholds, gates removed.
formulas: Daily Liquid Assets / Total Assets ≥ 25%.
Weekly Liquid Assets / Total Assets ≥ 50%.
Mandatory Fee Trigger: Daily Net Redemptions / NAV > 5%.
mnemonics: '25/50/5/2' = Daily 25%, Weekly 50%, Mandatory-fee trigger 5%, Discretionary cap 2%.

sections.title: V. Exchange-Traded Products (ETFs & ETNs)
sections.overview: ETPs trade intraday on exchanges and serve as alternatives to mutual funds. ETFs are typically registered investment companies (open-end or UIT structure) using a creation/redemption mechanism through authorized participants; ETNs are unsecured senior debt of issuers tracking an index.
key_concepts: ETFs: intraday trading; market price tracks NAV via in-kind creation/redemption by APs; passive (index) or active.
Lower expense ratios typically vs. comparable mutual funds; brokerage commissions may apply.
ETNs: unsecured debt obligations — investor bears issuer credit risk in addition to index performance risk; no principal protection unless stated.
Tax efficiency advantage common to ETFs due to in-kind redemption mechanism.
Marginable and shortable; options often available on widely held ETFs.
formulas: ETF Market Price ≈ iNAV (intraday indicative NAV); arbitrage by APs narrows the spread.
mnemonics: ETF = 'Equity-like Trading, Fund inside.' ETN = 'Exchange-Traded NOTE — creditor risk.'

sections.title: VI. Variable Contracts & Annuities
sections.overview: Variable annuities and variable life products are hybrid insurance-securities products. Subaccount values fluctuate with separate-account investments. They are securities under the '33 Act and insurance contracts under state law; FINRA Rule 2330 governs recommended deferred VA transactions.
key_concepts: Two phases: Accumulation (units purchased) and Annuitization/Payout (units converted to annuity units; payments vary with separate account performance vs. AIR).
Separate account holds investor assets and is registered as an investment company (typically UIT or open-end management).
Tax deferral on growth inside the contract; ordinary income on withdrawal of earnings; 10% penalty if withdrawn before 59½.
Surrender charges: declining schedule, often 6–8 years (CDSC).
Death benefit: typically greater of contract value or premiums paid (less withdrawals).
Riders: GLWB, GMIB, enhanced death benefit — at additional cost.
Prospectus delivery: Initial Summary Prospectus (ISP) permitted since 7/1/2020 (SEC Rel. 33-10765); full statutory prospectus online/on request.
Rule 2330 applies to recommended purchases/exchanges of deferred VAs and initial subaccount allocations; principal review and customer suitability disclosures required.
1035 exchange: tax-free exchange of like insurance contracts; FINRA scrutinizes exchanges for surrender charges, new surrender period, lost benefits.
rules: FINRA Rule 2330 — members' responsibilities regarding deferred variable annuities (suitability, disclosure, principal review).
SEC Rel. 33-10765 — Initial Summary Prospectus for variable contracts.
formulas: AIR (Assumed Interest Rate) Comparison: If actual separate-account return > AIR → next payment increases; if < AIR → decreases; if = AIR → unchanged.
Accumulation Unit Value fluctuates with subaccount performance.
Annuity Unit Value = fixed number of units × current unit value at payout.
mnemonics: VA = 'Variable Accumulation' phase then 'Variable Annuitization.'
AIR rule: 'Above AIR Adds, Below AIR Burns.'

sections.title: VII. Life Insurance Products (Insurance-Based)
sections.overview: Life insurance products provide death benefit protection; some build cash value. Variable and variable universal forms are securities and require both insurance and securities licensing to sell. Section 1035 of the IRC permits tax-free exchanges between like insurance contracts.
key_concepts: Term life: pure death benefit, no cash value; level or decreasing; renewable/convertible options.
Whole life: permanent coverage, fixed premium, guaranteed cash value, guaranteed minimum interest — NOT a security.
Universal life: flexible premium, adjustable death benefit, cash value earns current interest rate — NOT a security.
Variable life: fixed scheduled premium, death benefit and cash value vary with subaccount performance — IS a security; minimum guaranteed death benefit.
Variable Universal Life (VUL): flexible premium + subaccount investment; cash value and death benefit both variable; no guaranteed minimum death benefit unless stated rider — IS a security.
1035 Exchange: tax-free exchange of life insurance → life insurance or annuity; annuity → annuity (but NOT annuity → life insurance).
Variable life/VUL require prospectus delivery and registered representative licensing.
rules: FINRA Rule 2330 — applies to deferred variable annuities (life insurance variable contracts also regulated; suitability obligations apply).
mnemonics: 'Whole + Universal = Fixed insurance side; Variable + VUL = Securities side.'
1035 direction: 'Life → Life or Annuity; Annuity → Annuity ONLY.'

sections.title: VIII. Municipal Fund Securities (529s, LGIPs, ABLE)
sections.overview: Municipal fund securities are securities issued by state/municipal entities that would be investment companies but for §2(b) of the '40 Act. They include 529 college savings plans, prepaid tuition plans, ABLE accounts, and LGIPs, and are regulated by the MSRB.
key_concepts: 529 Savings Plans: investment-based; owner controls account; beneficiary uses funds for qualified education expenses; tax-deferred growth, tax-free qualified withdrawals (federal).
529 Prepaid Tuition: locks in tuition rates; usually state-residency requirements.
ABLE accounts: tax-advantaged savings for qualified disability expenses for eligible individuals.
LGIPs (Local Government Investment Pools): cash-management vehicles for municipalities.
Owner vs. Beneficiary: account owner retains control; beneficiary is the intended user of funds; owner may change beneficiary within family.
Direct-sold (state plan) vs. Adviser-sold (through broker-dealers with sales charges).
Home-state vs. out-of-state tax considerations — disclosure required.
Underlying mutual fund disclosures required under MSRB Rule G-45 reporting and Rule G-21 advertising standards.
rules: MSRB Rule D-12 — defines 'Municipal Fund Security' (security issued by issuer that, but for §2(b) of '40 Act, would be an investment company).
MSRB Rule G-17 — fair dealing, fundamental fair-practice obligation.
MSRB Rule G-45 — reporting on 529/ABLE plans by underwriters.
mnemonics: 529 = 'Save for Education, Account-owner-controlled.'
ABLE = 'Achieving a Better Life Experience' (disability-related).

sections.title: IX. Direct Participation Programs (DPPs)
sections.overview: DPPs are pooled investment vehicles, typically limited partnerships, that pass income, gains, losses, deductions, and credits directly to investors (flow-through taxation). They are generally illiquid, unlisted, and used for real estate, oil & gas, and equipment leasing.
key_concepts: Pass-through (flow-through) tax treatment — no entity-level tax.
Limited partnership: general partner (GP) manages and has unlimited liability; limited partners (LPs) are passive investors with limited liability up to invested capital.
Tenants in Common (TIC): co-ownership of real property, each holding undivided fractional interest.
Generally illiquid — no active secondary market.
Subscription agreement governs admission as LP; suitability standards are high.
Types: real estate (raw land, new construction, existing, government-assisted), oil & gas (exploratory, developmental, income), equipment leasing.
Excluded from DPP definition under Rule 2310: REITs, qualified pension/profit-sharing plans, IRAs, 403(b) annuities, registered investment companies.
rules: FINRA Rule 2310 — direct participation programs: suitability, due diligence, organization/offering expense limits, compensation limits.
formulas: Cash Flow = cash from operations (incl. net-lease payments) − operating expenses − debt service − capital improvements/replacements (no depreciation deducted).
Cash Available for Distribution = Cash Flow − reserves.
mnemonics: DPP = 'Direct Pass-through, Probably illiquid.'
GP/LP: 'GP runs and risks; LP funds and limits.'

sections.title: X. Real Estate Investment Trusts (REITs)
sections.overview: REITs are pooled investment vehicles holding real estate equity or mortgage debt that pass income to shareholders without entity-level tax if they meet IRC requirements. REITs are NOT DPPs and do not pass losses to investors.
key_concepts: Types by holdings: Equity REITs (own properties), Mortgage REITs (hold real-estate debt), Hybrid REITs.
Types by structure: Listed (exchange-traded, liquid), Registered Non-Listed (PNLR — registered but illiquid), Private (unregistered, accredited investors only).
To qualify under IRC: distribute at least 90% of taxable income; ≥75% of assets in real estate; ≥75% of gross income from real estate.
Single layer of taxation: distributions taxed at shareholder level (not entity).
Income passes through to investors; LOSSES DO NOT pass through (unlike DPPs).
Excluded from FINRA's DPP definition (Rule 2310).
formulas: REIT Distribution Test: ≥90% of taxable income distributed to shareholders.
Asset Test: ≥75% in real estate, cash, or government securities.
mnemonics: REIT = 'Real Estate Income, no Tax at entity (with 90% rule).'
'Income passes, Losses don't' — distinguishes REITs from DPPs.

sections.title: XI. Hedge Funds & Private Funds
sections.overview: Hedge funds are pooled, privately offered investment vehicles, typically structured as limited partnerships or LLCs, exempt from registration under the '40 Act. They use flexible strategies including leverage, short-selling, and derivatives, and are generally illiquid with high minimum investments.
key_concepts: Structure: limited partnership (manager = GP; investors = LPs) or LLC.
Reliance on '40 Act exemptions: §3(c)(1) (≤100 beneficial owners) or §3(c)(7) (qualified purchasers only).
Limited to accredited investors and qualified purchasers under Reg D.
High minimum investment; lockup periods; redemption gates and notice periods.
Performance/incentive fee plus management fee (commonly '2 and 20').
Not subject to mutual-fund-style leverage and diversification limits.
Private equity funds: similar structure but invest in non-public companies; long capital commitment periods.
Generally illiquid — no public secondary market.
rules: Investment Company Act of 1940 §3(c)(1) — exclusion when ≤100 beneficial owners and no public offering.
formulas: '2 and 20' = 2% annual management fee + 20% performance fee (typical).
High Water Mark: performance fee only on gains above previous peak NAV.
mnemonics: Hedge = 'High minimum, Highly illiquid, Highly leveraged.'

sections.title: XII. Investment Risks & Mitigation
sections.overview: Investments carry multiple risk types that registered representatives must identify and address through suitability analysis and portfolio strategy. Diversification, rebalancing, and hedging are the principal mitigation techniques.
key_concepts: Capital Risk: loss of principal.
Credit (Default) Risk: issuer fails to pay interest/principal.
Currency (FX) Risk: adverse exchange-rate movement on foreign-denominated assets.
Inflationary/Purchasing-Power Risk: erosion of real return; key risk for fixed-income.
Interest-Rate Risk: bond prices fall when rates rise (longer duration = greater sensitivity).
Reinvestment Risk: future cash flows reinvested at lower rates; greater for high-coupon callable bonds.
Liquidity (Marketability) Risk: inability to sell quickly at fair price; high for DPPs, hedge funds, non-listed REITs.
Market/Systematic Risk: cannot be diversified away; measured by beta.
Non-Systematic Risk: issuer/industry-specific; reducible via diversification.
Political/Legislative Risk: regulatory or governmental change impact.
Prepayment Risk: borrowers prepay loans (MBS) when rates fall; investor receives principal early.

Mitigation: Diversification (across asset classes, sectors, issuers, geographies); Portfolio Rebalancing (restore target allocations); Hedging (offset exposure via options, futures, inverse instruments).
formulas: Total Risk = Systematic Risk + Non-Systematic Risk.
Diversification reduces non-systematic risk but cannot eliminate systematic risk.
Real Return ≈ Nominal Return − Inflation Rate.
mnemonics: Risk types: 'C-CLIMP-RPP' — Capital, Credit, Currency, Liquidity, Inflation, Market, Political, Reinvestment, Prepayment, Purchasing-power.
'Diversify, Rebalance, Hedge' = the three mitigators.
Bonds: 'Rates Up → Prices Down' (seesaw).

sections.title: XIII. Disclosures & Customer Protection (Investment Company Context)
sections.overview: FINRA rules require members to make financial information available to customers and to disclose control relationships with issuers — duties particularly relevant when selling proprietary funds, affiliated REITs, or DPPs.
key_concepts: Members must make their most recent balance sheet available to bona fide regular customers upon request.

Members controlled by, controlling, or under common control with an issuer must disclose that relationship before executing transactions in that issuer's securities — written disclosure at or before completion of transaction.
Especially relevant to proprietary mutual funds, affiliated UITs, and DPPs sponsored by the broker-dealer's parent.
rules: FINRA Rule 2261 — Disclosure of Financial Condition (balance sheet on request).
FINRA Rule 2262 — Disclosure of Control Relationship with Issuer.
mnemonics: '2261 = my numbers; 2262 = my connection.'
